title: Amit Shah Chairs Southern CMs Conclave as Shivakumar Pushes Delimitation Resolution
excerpt: The Southern Zonal Council meeting near Mamallapuram brought together Chief Ministers from across southern India to address delimitation, NEET, Cauvery water sharing, and cooperative federalism.
body:
• Union Home Minister Amit Shah chaired the Southern Zonal Council meeting near Mamallapuram, Tamil Nadu, with Tamil Nadu CM C. Joseph Vijay as vice-chair
  • Karnataka CM D.K. Shivakumar pushed for a resolution to retain 543 Lok Sabha seats and honour the 1971 census as the basis for delimitation
  • Key issues discussed included NEET, delimitation, the Cauvery water dispute, the Mekedatu dam project, and cooperative federalism

Southern CMs Converge at Mamallapuram

Union Home Minister Amit Shah on Wednesday chaired the Southern Zonal Council meeting near Mamallapuram, Tamil Nadu, bringing together Chief Ministers from across southern India in a high-profile session dominated by demands for greater political representation and resource equity for the region.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=f8d7ScN452w

Tamil Nadu Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay served as vice-chair of the meeting, which included Karnataka CM D.K. Shivakumar, Andhra Pradesh CM N. Chandrababu Naidu, and representatives from Kerala, Telangana, and the southern Union Territories of Puducherry, Lakshadweep, and Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

The gathering marked a rare moment of bipartisan consensus, with leaders across party lines voicing concerns about the South's potential loss of political weight under a proposed delimitation exercise.

Shivakumar Pushes Delimitation Resolution

Karnataka CM Shivakumar emerged as one of the most vocal participants, calling on the Council to adopt a formal resolution to retain the current 543 Lok Sabha seats and use the 1971 census as the basis for any delimitation exercise, according to The Economic Times.

Shivakumar argued that southern states, which have successfully controlled population growth, should not be penalized through reduced parliamentary representation. He also called for accommodating women's reservation within the existing seat count rather than expanding the total.

"Give the South its due."

— D.K. Shivakumar, Chief Minister of Karnataka

The delimitation question is particularly sensitive for southern states. Under India's current system, parliamentary seats are distributed based on population. A fresh exercise using updated census data could shift seats northward, reducing the South's voice in Parliament despite the region's higher economic contributions and development indicators.

Vijay Bats for Cooperative Federalism

Tamil Nadu CM Vijay used the platform to advocate for cooperative federalism, asserting that "strong states make a stronger India," according to The Times of India. His agenda for the meeting included long-standing Tamil Nadu demands: opposition to NEET, concerns about delimitation, and the Cauvery water-sharing dispute.

Vijay's participation was closely watched as one of his first major inter-state engagements since taking office. His call for cooperative federalism echoed demands from multiple southern states for greater autonomy in education, healthcare, and fiscal policy.

Cauvery and Mekedatu on the Table

The perennial Cauvery water dispute featured prominently in discussions. Shivakumar told reporters that the proposed Mekedatu reservoir project in Karnataka would benefit not just his state but also Tamil Nadu and Puducherry by ensuring regulated monthly water releases to downstream regions.

Tamil Nadu has historically opposed the Mekedatu project, viewing it as a potential threat to its water allocation under existing tribunal awards. The Council meeting provided a forum for both sides to present their positions, though no binding resolution emerged on the water question.

What the Meeting Signals

The Southern Zonal Council, established under the States Reorganisation Act of 1956, is a statutory advisory body that facilitates dialogue between southern state governments and the Centre. While its recommendations are not binding, the Council serves as an important barometer of regional sentiment.

The meeting's focus on delimitation, fiscal devolution, and water sharing reflects growing assertiveness among southern states — many of which are net contributors to India's central tax pool but receive proportionally less in return.

For the Indian diaspora with roots in southern states, the outcomes carry direct relevance. Delimitation could reshape political representation for their home constituencies, while water-sharing agreements affect agriculture and daily life in regions where many NRI families maintain property and connections.
